title: Boot the Preview Worker from the shipped profile and fetch lazy chunks on demand
summary: The experimental browser Preview, which runs the whole host inside a Web Worker, boots from the same shipped profile as the served web deployment instead of a configuration dumped at pack time, and fetches lazy code chunks on demand.
firstReason: The Preview is possible because the upstream host is JavaScript and can run in a browser. Inference: a Go host could only do this compiled to WebAssembly, which no global decision plans. This first verdict must be confirmed by a recorded decision in the owning area, because DH-ADR-1 allows a part to be left out only that way.

title: Liveshare — sharing a DSH session with a colleague
summary: An owner can share a running session through a Liveshare server that both sides can reach. The reader opens a link and sees the session rendered by the owner's own host with its plugins, limited to that session and the children the reader creates; access is by organization link plus a deployment allow-list.
firstReason: DH-ADR-1 keeps experimental packages in scope. Because the page is rendered by the owner's host, a server-rendered UI should make the relay simpler than relaying a client application; the protocol itself may change under DH-ADR-2.

title: LiveShare plugin method catalog
summary: The list of plugin methods a share may expose to a viewer is read from the host's live method registry instead of being declared by each plugin. A share stores only per-method policies, and the host intersects each policy with that list before a call is dispatched; core methods and LiveShare's own methods are never in the list.
firstReason: One source of truth for what a share can grant closes the gap where a plugin's own declaration widened a viewer's reach. The rule is independent of the language: the Go host enumerates its own registered remote methods in place of the upstream Typert registry.

title: one host claims the LiveShare owner state
summary: When two host processes start on the same home directory, exactly one claims the LiveShare owner state by writing a small claim file. The holder registers and changes shares; every other host can read them, and its attempts to change them get a typed refusal instead of silently stealing the relay registrations.
firstReason: Two Go host processes on one home directory have the same problem, and the rules (no expiry, contention is a typed answer, a claim left by a dead process is reclaimed) are the ones the session write lease already uses.
